Vague feedback can leave a real question unresolved: what does the reader need to understand or do? Ask for one example that would let you test a change. Replaying the comment gives no evidence about your suffix or the quality of the draft.

Hearing "this passage feels unnatural", for example, you can ask whether the sentences are too long or the order of the story is unclear. sections.title: Quick answer

sections.body_md:
Introversion describes a tendency to direct attention and energy inward. Intuition gives more weight to patterns and possibilities when taking in information. Feeling gives more weight to values and effects on people when deciding. Perceiving describes a preference for keeping options open in the external world. See the [INFP base page](/en/personality/infp) for the four preferences and their limits.

In the [16Personalities framework](https://www.16personalities.com/articles/our-theory), Assertive and Turbulent are opposite ends of Identity, a dimension concerning self-confidence and response to pressure. Feeling describes a preference in how people make decisions. The -T suffix concerns how they tend to assess themselves, including before and after a decision.

Think about how you assessed your work after reading the feedback. Two people can reread a draft the same number of times and still feel very differently about the quality of their original work. The number of rereads cannot establish an A/T result.

Fi–Ne–Si–Te is a common type-dynamics notation for INFP. It lists dominant introverted Feeling (Fi), auxiliary extraverted Intuition (Ne), tertiary Sensing and inferior extraverted Thinking (Te). The Myers & Briggs Foundation lists both Si and Se for tertiary Sensing. A/T has no role in this theoretical notation, and the stack gives no basis for predicting ability or behaviour.

The boundary lies here: how much someone says, or whether they review after a meeting, cannot decide a suffix on its own. To see one reaction more clearly, look back at how confident you were in that judgement at the time, and which situational factors — load, deadline, experience, who was present — raised the pressure.
sections.title: INFP-T letters and framework

sections.body_md:
Specific feedback can give you something to check. A vague comment may leave you unsure whether the issue is an unfamiliar term, the order of ideas or the point of the passage. If you start doubting the whole draft, separate what the reader actually said from what you think it means about your work.

In this fictional draft review, a reader says, “This passage isn’t clear.” Ask which sentence or idea was hard to follow. Once you know where they got stuck, make a change that addresses that point. If the problem is still unclear, keep the draft and ask a fresh reader to try the same passage.

| Trigger | A tendency that may appear | An action to start with |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Hearing general criticism | Concern that the wording may have been unclear | Ask the other person to point to a specific passage and which sentence did not read smoothly first |
| No reply by the agreed time | Worry that the message was unclear | If a response is needed, check receipt through the agreed channel. Keep the reason for the silence unknown. |
| An omission appears | Concern that one omission casts doubt on the rest of the work | List who and which steps it affects, and fix the step with the largest effect first |
| Considering the same last-minute request | Concern that the other person may see a refusal as unhelpful | Check what you already agreed to and what you can do now before you answer. |
| After the same round of revisions | Uncertainty about whether the edited passage is clear | Have someone who has not read it verify once, and stop when there is no new problem |

There are opposite cases too. On a technical task you have done for a long time, you may receive one clearly wrong comment, find the reason within minutes and reply directly; on a first public presentation, the same kind of judgement takes several more rounds. Familiarity, verifiability and the load at the time can all change the intensity of this kind of reaction. Observing which tasks you can close decisively is more useful than counting how many times you replayed something in a day.
sections.title: INFP-T traits, strengths and blind spots

sections.body_md:
At work this reviewing can be put into a loop with boundaries: write the revision conditions first, then decide when to stop. It suits finding what was missed and does not suit being used as a reason to extend a deadline indefinitely — the difference lies in whether "how much change counts as finished" was agreed in advance.

In this fictional example, a mentor says the sign-up requirements are hard to read on your poster. Another student would prefer brighter colours. Ask a fresh reader to find the registration link and the deadline. If they get stuck, check placement, font size or information order. Decide whether the colour suggestion affects the same goal.

The revision is ready when a new reader can find the required information and follow the sign-up instructions. Agree a short window for the changes and check against that goal at the end. If feedback conflicts, ask the organiser which requirements apply. Ask the reader to show where they got stuck.

When exploring a job, ask how the team gives feedback and how it decides when a revision is complete. Ask for a recent example involving the kind of work you would actually do. Try a representative task and notice whether you want to repeat it, whether the feedback helps and which working conditions matter. Those observations give you more evidence about the role than the suffix does.

When feedback sits inside a grading or appraisal relationship, record suggestions and requirements separately. A mentor saying "you could add examples if you have time" and a grading rule stating "two examples are required" call for different actions. With conflicting comments, first ask whoever has authority to confirm the priority; you can also sort comments into must change this round, worth trying next round and no change needed, so that each round of revision corresponds to one clear purpose.

When the same piece of feedback recurs across several rounds of redrafting, turn it into a starting condition. If readers cannot find the date twice running, check the position of all required information before writing next time, moving part of the review cost to a point where adjustment is still possible.
sections.title: INFP-T work and career exploration

sections.body_md:
If you readily replay conversations in relationships, separate three things first: guilt, the responsibility already promised, and the need the other person actually stated. Guilt is a feeling, responsibility is a commitment, and need is the other person's situation at that moment; the three are often compressed into one sentence, "have I done something wrong".

In this fictional example, a housemate asks you to cover a shift at short notice. You decline and keep thinking about their reply, “It’s fine.” Check what you had agreed to. If you never agreed to cover, their need for help is separate from your refusal. If you had agreed, say what changed and clarify who will arrange and confirm cover.

When a friend replies very briefly, you can ask: "did what I said sound off to you? Let's talk when it suits you." That leaves room for an explanation and lets you learn whether what needs a response is the original sentence, the timing, or a misreading. Stop once the effect is handled; apologising repeatedly often shifts the work of reassuring you onto the other person.

If the other person really is disappointed, acknowledge that they need another arrangement, then give the range you can offer. For example, you are willing to pass the message on before dinner — that is a limited offer made separately, not the same as covering the shift tonight. Keeping sympathy and commitment apart makes the help deliverable, and gives the other person time to find an alternative.
sections.title: INFP-T relationships and communication

sections.body_md:
Reactions under pressure differ by person and by situation and cannot be inferred from a suffix. The first thing to do is write separately the current difficulty, the actions you control and the parts that need someone else's help — this step has nothing to do with personality, it only separates things that got mixed together.

When several pieces of negative feedback arrive within one week, write down the dates and the exact words, and look at them one by one to see whether the same problem is repeating or whether they come from different standards. With three hours left, do the item with the largest consequence first and hand the remaining changes and observations to whoever can decide. Record sleep, workload and deadlines alongside, so that a short-term load and a long-term assessment of yourself do not collapse into one sentence, "I am no good".

At the end of the day you can set a stopping point: note the first step for tomorrow, then close the old draft. If distress persistently affects sleep, work or relationships, appropriate psychological or medical support can be sought, describing the duration, intensity and scope of the effect; whether help is needed is judged from the real difficulty, not from a suffix.
sections.title: INFP-T stress and recovery

sections.body_md:
Use this exercise to understand how you respond to feedback and find out whether a specific revision helped. It has no A/T score. Take a comment you can quote accurately, turn it into a checkable question and see whether one change addresses it.

The method is to write three lines — what you wanted to achieve before receiving the comment, what the other person ran into, and the smallest change available right now. After the change, ask the person who commented to look once more and ask only one thing: is the place that was stuck still stuck. If there is no new problem, this round ends; if there is, first confirm whether it is the same problem, then decide whether to open another round.

The stopping condition has to be set in advance: the place has been changed, the agreed verification can be completed, and no new specific problem has appeared — when all three hold, stop. You can also keep a separate column for the things you worried about at the time that never happened. They are not mistakes but observation clues — for example, the more abstract the comment, the stronger the wish to redo it, and with an example it can stop quickly. Once a pattern like that is visible, you can ask for clearer feedback next time.

sections.body_md:
**Framework sources.** The [NERIS account of Identity](https://www.16personalities.com/articles/identity-assertive-vs-turbulent) defines Assertive and Turbulent. The [16Personalities model overview](https://www.16personalities.com/articles/our-theory) explains where Identity sits in that instrument. The Myers & Briggs Foundation describes the four official MBTI preferences and type dynamics. The two frameworks use some of the same letters, but this gives no basis for converting scores or interpretations between them.

**Function notation.** This page uses Fi–Ne–Si–Te, a common notation for INFP. The Myers & Briggs Foundation identifies the third process as Sensing and lists both Si and Se. Those positions describe roles in a theory and cannot tell you how someone will perform or react to pressure.

**Editorial fiction statement** The sign-up poster with the two comments from a mentor and a fellow student, the housemate's last-minute shift and the "it's fine", the friend's very short reply, passing a message on before dinner, several pieces of negative feedback within one week, and the redrafting back and forth over "this passage is not clear enough" are all episodes invented by the editors to explain the practice, and correspond to no real person or event.

**Scope limits** When interpreting a result, the answering situation, the load and the experience can be taken into account, and the result is not for hiring screening, relationship prediction or ranking ability. This page offers no method of typing and no rehabilitation or treatment advice; matters involving health and safety should follow the guidance of a qualified professional. See the [assessment method and evidence notes](/en/tests/mbti-personality-test-16-personality-types#method-and-evidence).

The FermatMind editorial team

sections.body_md:
In INFP-T, -T means Turbulent, the end of 16Personalities’ NERIS Identity dimension associated with more self-doubt and greater sensitivity to pressure or feedback. Official MBTI uses four preference pairs. A T in the third position of a four-letter code means Thinking. The third letter of INFP is F for Feeling.

INFP stands for Introversion, Intuition, Feeling and Perceiving. The suffix leaves those preferences unchanged. Someone can feel less confident after criticism and still make the same checks and revisions as someone who feels more confident.

The other end of 16Personalities’ Identity dimension is Assertive. The examples below use criticism, declining a request and revising a draft to separate self-assessment from what actually happened. None can establish a suffix, assess ability or diagnose anxiety.

| Core profile | INFP-T |
| --- | --- |
| Four letters | I introversion, N intuition, F a feeling preference in judgement, P perceiving |
| The T after the hyphen | Turbulent, one end of the NERIS Identity dimension |
| What it is not | Not a fifth official MBTI dimension, not Thinking, not among the four letters |
| What this end describes | Self-assessment, self-assurance and sensitivity to pressure; it measures no quality of judgement |
| Where it may show | Less certainty about one’s own assessment when feedback is vague, responsibility is unclear or a deadline is close |
| A possible self-assessment | Taking one specific criticism as a reason to doubt your work more broadly |
| An action to start with | Write the worry as one testable statement and agree the stopping condition in advance |
sections.title: Quick answer

sections.body_md:
Introversion describes a tendency to direct attention and energy inward. Intuition gives more weight to patterns and possibilities when taking in information. Feeling gives more weight to values and effects on people when deciding. Perceiving describes a preference for keeping options open in the external world. See the [INFP base page](/en/personality/infp) for the four preferences and their limits.

In the [16Personalities framework](https://www.16personalities.com/articles/our-theory), Assertive and Turbulent are opposite ends of Identity, a dimension concerning self-confidence and response to pressure. Feeling describes a preference in how people make decisions. The -T suffix concerns how they tend to assess themselves, including before and after a decision.

Think about how you assessed your work after reading the feedback. Two people can reread a draft the same number of times and still feel very differently about the quality of their original work. The number of rereads cannot establish an A/T result.

Fi–Ne–Si–Te is a common type-dynamics notation for INFP. It lists dominant introverted Feeling (Fi), auxiliary extraverted Intuition (Ne), tertiary Sensing and inferior extraverted Thinking (Te). The Myers & Briggs Foundation lists both Si and Se for tertiary Sensing. A/T has no role in this theoretical notation, and the stack gives no basis for predicting ability or behaviour.

The boundary lies here: how much someone says, or whether they review after a meeting, cannot decide a suffix on its own. To see one reaction more clearly, look back at how confident you were in that judgement at the time, and which situational factors — load, deadline, experience, who was present — raised the pressure.
sections.title: INFP-T letters and framework

sections.body_md:
Specific feedback can give you something to check. A vague comment may leave you unsure whether the issue is an unfamiliar term, the order of ideas or the point of the passage. If you start doubting the whole draft, separate what the reader actually said from what you think it means about your work.

In this fictional draft review, a reader says, “This passage isn’t clear.” Ask which sentence or idea was hard to follow. Once you know where they got stuck, make a change that addresses that point. If the problem is still unclear, keep the draft and ask a fresh reader to try the same passage.

| Trigger | A tendency that may appear | An action to start with |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Hearing general criticism | Concern that the wording may have been unclear | Ask the other person to point to a specific passage and which sentence did not read smoothly first |
| No reply by the agreed time | Worry that the message was unclear | If a response is needed, check receipt through the agreed channel. Keep the reason for the silence unknown. |
| An omission appears | Concern that one omission casts doubt on the rest of the work | List who and which steps it affects, and fix the step with the largest effect first |
| Considering the same last-minute request | Concern that the other person may see a refusal as unhelpful | Check what you already agreed to and what you can do now before you answer. |
| After the same round of revisions | Uncertainty about whether the edited passage is clear | Have someone who has not read it verify once, and stop when there is no new problem |

There are opposite cases too. On a technical task you have done for a long time, you may receive one clearly wrong comment, find the reason within minutes and reply directly; on a first public presentation, the same kind of judgement takes several more rounds. Familiarity, verifiability and the load at the time can all change the intensity of this kind of reaction. Observing which tasks you can close decisively is more useful than counting how many times you replayed something in a day.
sections.title: INFP-T traits, strengths and blind spots

sections.body_md:
At work this reviewing can be put into a loop with boundaries: write the revision conditions first, then decide when to stop. It suits finding what was missed and does not suit being used as a reason to extend a deadline indefinitely — the difference lies in whether "how much change counts as finished" was agreed in advance.

In this fictional example, a mentor says the sign-up requirements are hard to read on your poster. Another student would prefer brighter colours. Ask a fresh reader to find the registration link and the deadline. If they get stuck, check placement, font size or information order. Decide whether the colour suggestion affects the same goal.

The revision is ready when a new reader can find the required information and follow the sign-up instructions. Agree a short window for the changes and check against that goal at the end. If feedback conflicts, ask the organiser which requirements apply. Ask the reader to show where they got stuck.

When exploring a job, ask how the team gives feedback and how it decides when a revision is complete. Ask for a recent example involving the kind of work you would actually do. Try a representative task and notice whether you want to repeat it, whether the feedback helps and which working conditions matter. Those observations give you more evidence about the role than the suffix does.

When feedback sits inside a grading or appraisal relationship, record suggestions and requirements separately. A mentor saying "you could add examples if you have time" and a grading rule stating "two examples are required" call for different actions. With conflicting comments, first ask whoever has authority to confirm the priority; you can also sort comments into must change this round, worth trying next round and no change needed, so that each round of revision corresponds to one clear purpose.

When the same piece of feedback recurs across several rounds of redrafting, turn it into a starting condition. If readers cannot find the date twice running, check the position of all required information before writing next time, moving part of the review cost to a point where adjustment is still possible.
sections.title: INFP-T work and career exploration

sections.body_md:
If you readily replay conversations in relationships, separate three things first: guilt, the responsibility already promised, and the need the other person actually stated. Guilt is a feeling, responsibility is a commitment, and need is the other person's situation at that moment; the three are often compressed into one sentence, "have I done something wrong".

In this fictional example, a housemate asks you to cover a shift at short notice. You decline and keep thinking about their reply, “It’s fine.” Check what you had agreed to. If you never agreed to cover, their need for help is separate from your refusal. If you had agreed, say what changed and clarify who will arrange and confirm cover.

When a friend replies very briefly, you can ask: "did what I said sound off to you? Let's talk when it suits you." That leaves room for an explanation and lets you learn whether what needs a response is the original sentence, the timing, or a misreading. Stop once the effect is handled; apologising repeatedly often shifts the work of reassuring you onto the other person.

If the other person really is disappointed, acknowledge that they need another arrangement, then give the range you can offer. For example, you are willing to pass the message on before dinner — that is a limited offer made separately, not the same as covering the shift tonight. Keeping sympathy and commitment apart makes the help deliverable, and gives the other person time to find an alternative.
sections.title: INFP-T relationships and communication

sections.body_md:
Reactions under pressure differ by person and by situation and cannot be inferred from a suffix. The first thing to do is write separately the current difficulty, the actions you control and the parts that need someone else's help — this step has nothing to do with personality, it only separates things that got mixed together.

When several pieces of negative feedback arrive within one week, write down the dates and the exact words, and look at them one by one to see whether the same problem is repeating or whether they come from different standards. With three hours left, do the item with the largest consequence first and hand the remaining changes and observations to whoever can decide. Record sleep, workload and deadlines alongside, so that a short-term load and a long-term assessment of yourself do not collapse into one sentence, "I am no good".

At the end of the day you can set a stopping point: note the first step for tomorrow, then close the old draft. If distress persistently affects sleep, work or relationships, appropriate psychological or medical support can be sought, describing the duration, intensity and scope of the effect; whether help is needed is judged from the real difficulty, not from a suffix.
sections.title: INFP-T stress and recovery

sections.body_md:
Use this exercise to understand how you respond to feedback and find out whether a specific revision helped. It has no A/T score. Take a comment you can quote accurately, turn it into a checkable question and see whether one change addresses it.

The method is to write three lines — what you wanted to achieve before receiving the comment, what the other person ran into, and the smallest change available right now. After the change, ask the person who commented to look once more and ask only one thing: is the place that was stuck still stuck. If there is no new problem, this round ends; if there is, first confirm whether it is the same problem, then decide whether to open another round.

The stopping condition has to be set in advance: the place has been changed, the agreed verification can be completed, and no new specific problem has appeared — when all three hold, stop. You can also keep a separate column for the things you worried about at the time that never happened. They are not mistakes but observation clues — for example, the more abstract the comment, the stronger the wish to redo it, and with an example it can stop quickly. Once a pattern like that is visible, you can ask for clearer feedback next time.
sections.title: INFP-T observation practice

sections.body_md:
- [INFP four-letter base page](/en/personality/infp): the full account of the I, N, F and P preferences and the function reading.
- [INFP-A](/en/personality/infp-a): shares the same four letters, and the difference lies only at the right end of the hyphen — the A end is usually less disturbed by pressure, the T end usually more prone to self-doubt.
- [INFP-A and INFP-T same-type comparison](/en/personality/infp-a-vs-infp-t): the same piece of feedback and the same responsibility, and where each end starts.
- [Browse the personality directory](/en/personality): the entry point to the introductory pages of other types.
sections.title: INFP-T related types and comparisons

items.answer:
It means Turbulent, one end of the Identity dimension in the NERIS system used by 16Personalities, opposed to Assertive; it is not among the four letters and does not measure ability.

If you want to reflect on confidence under pressure, compare a few situations with different stakes or levels of experience. Note what you knew at the time and how confident you felt. The notes describe your experience and cannot tell you whether you have an A or T result.
items.question: What does the T in INFP-T mean?

items.answer:
No. T is a NERIS suffix; it cannot be used to judge whether someone has an anxiety problem, nor to conclude that someone belongs to what is usually called high sensitivity.

If worry is affecting your sleep, work or relationships, note when it began, how long it has lasted and what it interferes with. You can use those observations when discussing it with a qualified professional. The suffix establishes neither an anxiety disorder nor a sensitivity trait.
items.question: Is INFP-T the same as anxiety or high sensitivity?

items.answer:
Vague feedback can leave a real question unresolved: what does the reader need to understand or do? Ask for one example that would let you test a change. Replaying the comment gives no evidence about your suffix or the quality of the draft.

Hearing "this passage feels unnatural", for example, you can ask whether the sentences are too long or the order of the story is unclear. Once you have a specific place, change one thing only and ask the other person to confirm; when the problem cannot yet be stated clearly, keep the draft and the question and wait for the material to be complete, which controls the time spent better than repeated rewriting. It may also simply have been a few nights of little sleep — that kind of condition is worth recording too.
items.question: What can help when you keep revisiting criticism?

items.answer:
Separate guilt from commitment first: guilt is a feeling, commitment is a fact, and only the latter needs an account.

If you promised to send a file before three, say when it can be sent late; if an added request exceeds your capacity, you can say plainly that you cannot take it on now and leave the other person room to decide on an alternative. If you never agreed, "I cannot do it tonight" is enough, and there is no need to count the other person's disappointment as your breach.
items.question: What should I do about guilt after refusing a request?

items.answer:
Yes. How fast a decision is made depends more on whether the task is familiar, how large the cost is and whether the feedback can be verified than on the suffix.

With a clear standard you may finish checking quickly; when the premise is unclear, asking one more question is reasonable. To understand your own rhythm, record a few real decisions: what they rested on, how long they took, and whether the result matched the original requirement. The quality of a judgement is judged by how well the result matches the requirement, not by how long you hesitated.
items.question: Can INFP-T be decisive?

items.answer:
Using whether a reader can complete the specified action as the stopping point is more reliable than waiting until you no longer feel worried.

For a sign-up note, give it to someone who has not read it and ask them to find the time and the entry; if they can follow the steps, keep the current version. If one piece of information is still wrong, change only the relevant sentence and ask them to look again. The basis for ending is that the agreed requirement has been verified, not that it finally feels perfect.
items.question: How do I know I can stop redrafting?

items.answer:
Possibly. The experience you draw on in different situations affects the answers, but a change in the suffix result does not mean the personality itself changed.

To compare two results, first confirm whether it was the same tool, the same version and the same language; if the same tool reports dimension scores, see whether the result sits near the dividing line, and dividing lines from different tools should not be compared directly. You can also note what you were thinking about at each sitting — one based on familiar daily life, one just after public criticism — as a clue for understanding the difference.
items.question: Can INFP-T change because the two test situations were different?

items.answer:
Choose by the layer you have not yet settled: the four letters, the other end, or a side-by-side comparison in the same situation.

The four letters and the function reading are on the [INFP base page](/en/personality/infp); the definition of the other end is on [INFP-A](/en/personality/infp-a); the difference between the two ends facing the same feedback and the same responsibility is on the [same-type comparison](/en/personality/infp-a-vs-infp-t). Taking one recent small event with you makes it easier to find the part you can use.
items.question: After reading INFP-T, which page comes next?

sections.body_md:
**Framework sources.** The [NERIS account of Identity](https://www.16personalities.com/articles/identity-assertive-vs-turbulent) defines Assertive and Turbulent. The [16Personalities model overview](https://www.16personalities.com/articles/our-theory) explains where Identity sits in that instrument. The Myers & Briggs Foundation describes the four official MBTI preferences and type dynamics. The two frameworks use some of the same letters, but this gives no basis for converting scores or interpretations between them.

**Function notation.** This page uses Fi–Ne–Si–Te, a common notation for INFP. The Myers & Briggs Foundation identifies the third process as Sensing and lists both Si and Se. Those positions describe roles in a theory and cannot tell you how someone will perform or react to pressure.

**Editorial fiction statement** The sign-up poster with the two comments from a mentor and a fellow student, the housemate's last-minute shift and the "it's fine", the friend's very short reply, passing a message on before dinner, several pieces of negative feedback within one week, and the redrafting back and forth over "this passage is not clear enough" are all episodes invented by the editors to explain the practice, and correspond to no real person or event.

**Scope limits** When interpreting a result, the answering situation, the load and the experience can be taken into account, and the result is not for hiring screening, relationship prediction or ranking ability. This page offers no method of typing and no rehabilitation or treatment advice; matters involving health and safety should follow the guidance of a qualified professional. See the [assessment method and evidence notes](/en/tests/mbti-personality-test-16-personality-types#method-and-evidence).

The FermatMind editorial team
